title: The earth
hookLine: don't waste, don't destroy, care for the land
tomorrow: Noa's cat-sitting for Mr. Feld. is the rule about the cat, or her?

lines: THE SET GOES IN A DUMPSTER.
"IS THE TREE OF THE FIELD MAN?"
cards: After the last show comes strike, and a whole set goes into a dumpster: painted flats, a staircase, a door that opened every night. Now an odd line.
In the middle of the Torah's laws of war, a city under siege, the text stops to talk about trees. Don't cut down the fruit trees, it says.
Then it asks a strange question, in the JPS 1917 translation: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?"

teach.b: So why does a war law stop for trees? Part of the answer is in the question. The tree isn't your enemy.

It can't run behind the walls, and it didn't start this. Even at war there's a line: you don't destroy what feeds people just because you can. The rabbis carried that line out of the battlefield and into the house.
They called it bal tashchit, do not destroy, and the Talmud stretches it to things like wasting a lamp's oil or ruining good clothes for no reason. Then a second verse widens it again.
About the land, God says in Leviticus: "for the land is Mine." The people living on it are tenants, sharing it with each other and with whoever comes next. A midrash makes it tender.
God walks Adam through the garden and shows him the trees: see how beautiful they are.
Take care not to ruin My world, because if you ruin it, there is no one to repair it after you.
Lived, the earth looks ordinary: the set flats reused for the next show, the shoes resoled, the leftovers eaten, the faucet off while you brush.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Torah's rule against waste starts in the middle of a war.

how: Many Jews cite bal tashchit, the rule against needless destruction, when they talk about waste and the environment; Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees, is often marked with tree planting and care for the land.

o: a farm owned together by a whole town
the ground on which a synagogue is built
the world as a gift on loan, not ours to ruin

p: not your enemy in a siege

s: the Torah's rule about trees is set in peacetime
it's set in the middle of a siege: even at war, don't cut down the fruit trees.
the rabbis stretched bal tashchit past trees to other waste
the Talmud applies it to wasting lamp oil and ruining good clothes.
caring for the earth has no roots in the Torah itself
Deuteronomy protects the fruit trees, Leviticus says 'the land is Mine', and a midrash has God warning Adam not to ruin the world.

games.q: your shul is renovating and plans to toss the old wooden benches. by bal tashchit, what's the first move?
o: find someone who can use them before anything goes in a dumpster.
toss them: the rule is about fruit trees, not furniture.
keep them in storage for good, even if nobody uses them.
games.why: the rabbis stretched the fruit-tree law to anything still useful. the question is whether it can still give, not whether it's a tree.

practice: Pick up one thing near you that's headed for the trash: a jar, a box, a half-used notebook. Turn it over in your hands for a few slow breaths. Ask it the Torah's kind of question: is it finished, or only finished for me?

wordCard.voice: The earth: a world on loan, with a line even war doesn't cross. Don't destroy what can still give.

orig.note: Hebrew: do not destroy; the rabbis' name for the rule against needless waste.

carryVoice: Worth keeping: the land is shared, with your neighbors and with whoever comes next. Nine of twenty.

sources.q: for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 67b (wasting lamp oil); Kiddushin 32a (tearing garments) as bal tashchit
Ecclesiastes Rabbah 7:13 (God shows Adam the trees: do not ruin My world, for no one will repair it after you)
